intro:
This track opens up a database and builds its insides one part at a time. Lessons start from scenes everyone knows: a card payment that must survive a power cut, a phone that stays full after you delete photos, the index at the back of a cookbook, a café owner with a shoebox of receipts. Then they open up the machinery, with real bytes from PostgreSQL's files and small pieces of a database that you build yourself.

By the end, you can follow one card payment from the moment a program saves it down to the bytes on the drive, and back up through the question that reads it:

- when a save is really on the drive, and what a crash can and can't take away;
- how a table becomes a file of 8 KB pages, and which pages a database keeps in memory;
- why an index is a short, wide tree, and when a stack of sorted files (an LSM tree) fits better;
- how the write-ahead log lets a database crash at any moment and come back whole;
- which index answers questions about words, time, places on a map and meaning;
- how a database runs a plan, and how it picks one plan out of many by guessing row counts;
- why reports read columns, and when a stored answer beats asking the question again;
- how two real databases, Neo4j and a PostgreSQL server, put the parts together.

In practice, you can read PostgreSQL's report on a query (`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`) and its statistics, say what the database is doing and why, and know which index or setting to change.

The fourteen lessons:

1. Bytes, pages and durability: a log-structured store
2. Pages, tuples and heap files
3. The buffer pool
4. B+trees
5. LSM trees, SSTables and Bloom filters
6. Write-ahead logging and crash recovery
7. Indexes and reading EXPLAIN
8. Indexes for text, time and vectors
9. Query execution: iterators, joins and vectors
10. Query optimization and cardinality estimates
11. Column stores and compression
12. Materialized views and data cubes
13. Inside Neo4j: native graph storage, memory and clustering
14. Running PostgreSQL: processes, configuration, roles and connections

You need to read a little code, in Kotlin or Java, and to have Docker and JDK 25 on your laptop. Docker is a free program that runs small, separate Linux systems, called containers, on your own computer. The labs compile for Java 21, so JDK 21 or newer runs them. You don't need any database background: every term is explained the first time it appears. The SQL track's lessons on joins, aggregation and JDBC come up here, and the Operating systems track's lessons on processes and the page cache come back in lessons 1, 3 and 14.

Most labs live in `labs/internals`, one package per lesson (`sfz.store.l01` to `sfz.store.l12`). In each one you build a piece of a storage engine in plain Kotlin: a store that only adds to the end of one file, a slotted page, a buffer pool, a B+tree, an LSM store, a write-ahead log, a plan runner, a row-count guesser that orders joins, a compressed column chunk and a view that keeps itself up to date. They need no Docker, and their tests give the same answer every time, pretend crashes included. Lessons 8 and 13 model a word index, a vector search and Neo4j's record files in `labs/nosql`, also without Docker. Lessons 7 and 14 test SQL and server settings against PostgreSQL 18 in `labs/sql`, which needs Docker. Run `./gradlew :internals:test --tests 'sfz.store.l05.*'` from `labs/` for one lesson; the finished answers live in `src/solution`. The Try its run PostgreSQL 18 from `labs/env/postgres.yml`, the other programs a lesson names (the search engine OpenSearch, the PostgreSQL add-ons TimescaleDB and pgvector, and Neo4j), and small demos, one of which runs the column database DuckDB inside a Java program.
cheatsheet:
## The track on one page

| # | Lesson | The problem | The mechanism | Remember |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A log-structured store | `write` returns before the data is on the drive | add every record to the end of one file; `force` (fsync); a checksum (CRC) per record; a map of keys in memory (the keydir); merging | reply OK only after the force; the keydir must fit in memory and keeps no order |
| 2 | Pages and heap files | rows of any length in fixed 8 KB pages | slotted page: slots (line pointers) at the front, rows at the back; a row's address is (page, slot) | DELETE and plain VACUUM don't shrink the file |
| 3 | The buffer pool | a read from the drive costs far more than one from memory | frames, a page table, pins, dirty flags, the clock sweep, a small ring for big scans | a pinned page is never thrown out; `shared_buffers` near 25% of RAM |
| 4 | B+trees | one row out of millions in a few reads | a short, wide sorted tree of pages; splits; linked leaves; copy-on-write in LMDB | 3 or 4 levels; exact matches on the first columns, then one range |
| 5 | LSM trees | scattered inserts rewrite whole pages | a sorted table in memory (memtable), sorted files that never change (SSTables), Bloom filters, compaction | about 10 bits per key for 1% wrong "maybe"s; leveled compaction rewrites data 10 times or more |
| 6 | Write-ahead logging | pages reach the drive long after the commit | log before page, force the log at commit, a log position (LSN) on every page, redo from a checkpoint, full-page copies | `synchronous_commit = off` may lose the last commits; `fsync = off` may corrupt |
| 7 | Indexes and EXPLAIN | 14 rows without reading every page | index entries point at table rows; indexes on several columns, INCLUDE, partial and expression indexes | read EXPLAIN from the most indented step up; rows x loops; a cast on the column stops the index |
| 8 | Indexes for text, time and vectors | questions with no single sort order | posting lists in Lucene segments, time chunks and rollups, geohash, R-trees (GiST), H3, HNSW, DiskANN | approximate indexes can miss; pgvector filters after the HNSW walk |
| 9 | Query execution | running a plan without holding whole results | steps that pull one row at a time (iterators); nested loop, hash and merge joins; vectorized and compiled engines | batches of about 1,000 values; compiling can cost more than a short query |
| 10 | Query optimization | dozens of plans for three tables | a cost model, row-count guesses (cardinality estimates), dynamic programming over groups of tables | a bad plan usually means a bad guess; `CREATE STATISTICS` for columns that go together |
| 11 | Column stores | a report reads every column of every row | columns stored apart; dictionary, run-length and bit-packing encodings; zone maps; micro-partitions | zone maps skip data only when it's sorted or clustered by the filter column |
| 12 | Materialized views and data cubes | the same costly total, asked all day | stored results, REFRESH (CONCURRENTLY), delta rules, GROUP BY CUBE | refresh cost follows the data, deltas follow the change; a deleted minimum needs the table |
| 13 | Inside Neo4j | following links without index searches | fixed-size records, doubly linked relationship chains, a page cache, a transaction log | record N sits at byte N x size; page cache = files + indexes + 20% |
| 14 | Running PostgreSQL | one server that survives real use | the postmaster and a process per connection, shared memory, pg_hba.conf, roles, PgBouncer | the first matching pg_hba line decides; postmaster settings need a restart; pool connections |

## Which structure answers which question

| The question | The structure | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| this key, this range, this prefix | B+tree | 4, 7 |
| many scattered writes, reads mostly by key | LSM tree | 5 |
| documents with these words, best first | inverted index, ranked with BM25 | 8 |
| a time range, added up | time chunks, buckets of count, sum, min and max | 8 |
| everything inside this box, nearest to this point | R-tree on GiST, geohash prefix, H3 cell | 8 |
| similar in meaning (close embeddings, lists of numbers) | HNSW, IVF, DiskANN, with compressed vectors | 8 |
| a few columns of millions of rows | column store with zone maps | 11 |
| the same total, many times | materialized view, kept up to date one change at a time if it can be | 12 |
| the neighbours of this node | record chains (Neo4j) | 13 |

## Numbers to keep

| What | Value |
|---|---|
| PostgreSQL page | 8 KB; row header 24 bytes, line pointer (slot) 4 bytes |
| B+tree | hundreds of keys per page, so 3 or 4 levels for any table |
| Bloom filter | 10 bits per key and 7 hash functions: about 1% wrong "maybe"s |
| Checkpoints, PostgreSQL 18 | `checkpoint_timeout` 5 min, `max_wal_size` 1 GB |
| Planner cost units | page read in order 1.0, page read out of order 4.0, row 0.01, operator 0.0025 |
| ANALYZE | 30,000 sampled rows; the 100 most common values and 100 histogram buckets at the default target of 100 |
| Join guess | rows(R) x rows(S) / max(distinct R.x, distinct S.y) |
| Join Order Benchmark | 52% of PostgreSQL's guesses for three joins off by 10 times or more |
| BM25 | k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75 |
| pgvector HNSW | `m` 16, `ef_construction` 64, `hnsw.ef_search` 40; iterative scans since 0.8.0 |
| Vectorized batches | X100: about 1,000 values best; DuckDB: 2,048 |
| Zone map size | DuckDB row group 122,880 rows; BRIN 128 pages; Snowflake micro-partition 50 to 500 MB; Redshift block 1 MB |
| Hash table memory | `work_mem` (4 MB) x `hash_mem_multiplier` (2) |
| Neo4j records | node 15 bytes, relationship 34, property 41 |
| A PostgreSQL connection | one process; about 1.5 MB of private memory when idle; `max_connections` 100 by default |

## Easy to confuse

| | One | The other |
|---|---|---|
| B+tree or LSM tree | changes pages in place; a read follows one path down; a scattered insert rewrites a whole page | adds to a table in memory and writes sorted files; writes are long and in order; a read may check several files, and compaction rewrites data |
| Buffer pool or the operating system's page cache | the database's own cache: it knows pins, dirty pages and the log rule | the kernel's cache of file data; PostgreSQL reads through it too, so a page can be cached twice |
| Exact or approximate index | B+tree, GiST: every match, always | HNSW, IVF: fast, but they can miss matches, and filters run after the walk |
| Nested loop or hash join | outer x inner work, or one index lookup per outer row; any condition; best for few outer rows | outer + inner work; equality only; needs memory for the table it builds |
| Vectorized or compiled | ready-made steps over batches of values; better at hiding waits for memory; no compile time | one generated loop per pipeline; fewer instructions; pays to compile each query |
| Zone map (BRIN) or B+tree | min and max per range of pages: tiny, helps only columns that follow the row order | an entry per row: precise in any order, much bigger |
| Index or materialized view | a copy of rows in another order | a copy of a worked-out answer; out of date until refreshed or kept up to date |
| REFRESH or REFRESH CONCURRENTLY | locks the view so readers wait (ACCESS EXCLUSIVE); usually less work | needs a unique index; readers keep reading; reruns the query, then applies the differences |

## Looking inside PostgreSQL

| To see | Use |
|---|---|
| the rows and slots of a page | `SELECT * FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('t', 0))` (pageinspect) |
| what is in memory | `pg_buffercache`, and `Buffers: shared hit / read` in `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` |
| an index's pages | `bt_metap`, `bt_page_items` (pageinspect) |
| the write-ahead log | `pg_current_wal_lsn()`, `pg_waldump` |
| what a plan did | `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)`: the guessed `rows=` against `actual rows=`, times `loops` |
| what the planner knows | `pg_stats`, `pg_stats_ext`; fix columns that go together with `CREATE STATISTICS` |
| what JIT compiled | the `JIT:` section of `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` (shown only with costs) |
| who holds a lock on a view | `pg_locks` filtered on `relation = 'name'::regclass` |
| how a setting changes | `pg_settings.context`, then `pending_restart` after `SELECT pg_reload_conf()` |
| who may connect | `pg_hba_file_rules`, checked before every reload |

## When something goes wrong, ask first

- Data lost after a crash: was the OK sent before a force, or with `synchronous_commit = off`?
- A query got slow: in EXPLAIN ANALYZE, which is the lowest step whose guessed and actual rows differ by 10 times or more?
- A vector search returns too few rows: is a WHERE clause filtering after the index walk?
- A dashboard freezes every few minutes: is a plain REFRESH locking its view?
- Reports slow down the database the app uses: can the scan move to a column store, loaded in batches and sorted by the filter column?
- New copies of a program fail with `remaining connection slots are reserved`: do the pools add up to more than `max_connections`?
- A graph walk got slow as the graph grew: does Neo4j's page cache still hold the files and indexes?
recap: A save is on the drive only after `force` (fsync) returns. A log makes that affordable: add each record to the end of one file, force once for many records, and check each record's checksum after a crash.

Tables are files of 8 KB pages, and a slotted page keeps rows of any length behind slot numbers, so a row's address is (page, slot). The buffer pool keeps busy pages in memory with pins, dirty flags and a clock sweep, on top of the operating system's own page cache.

A B+tree finds a key by reading one page per level, three or four in all, and changes pages in place. An LSM tree turns scattered writes into long sorted files and pays with merging (compaction) and reads that may check several files. No design wins on reads, writes and space at once.

The write-ahead log is forced to disk at commit and always reaches it before the pages it describes. After a crash, recovery replays it from the last checkpoint, and the log position (LSN) on each page makes replaying twice safe.

Every index is a copy of the data arranged for one shape of question: a B+tree for one sort order, posting lists for words, time chunks for time, R-trees and grid cells for maps, and graphs such as HNSW for meaning. Each costs work on every write, and the approximate ones can miss.

A plan is a tree of steps that pull rows one at a time. A nested loop costs outer x inner (or one index lookup per outer row), and a hash join about outer + inner. Engines that pass batches of values, or compile each query, cut the cost per row, and compiling has a cost of its own.

The planner prices the plans it considers and keeps the cheapest for its guesses of row counts. Guesses fail most on columns that go together and on joins, so fix the lowest guess that's far off before forcing a plan.

A column store keeps each column together, squeezes it small, and skips chunks by their smallest and largest values. Cloud warehouses skip data the same way, so the order data is loaded in decides how much a query reads.

A materialized view stores a query's answer and trades work on every write for cheap reads. A refresh redoes everything; keeping it up to date one change at a time is easy for counts and sums, and hard for minimums under deletes, for joins and for big batches. A data cube stores the totals for every combination of its dimensions.

Real databases are these parts put together. Neo4j is fixed-size records behind a page cache and a transaction log, and a PostgreSQL server is a process per connection around shared memory and a write-ahead log, guarded by pg_hba.conf and roles.

quiz.q: A program that records payments writes each one with Java's `FileChannel.write` and replies OK at once. The machine loses power a millisecond later. What may have happened to the payment?
options: Nothing: `write` returned, so the bytes are on the drive
It may be lost: `write` only copied it into the kernel's page cache in memory, and only `force` waits for the drive
It's half-written, and the next start fails
It's safe if the file was opened in append mode
quiz.why: `write` returns once the kernel, the core of the operating system, has the bytes in memory. They reach the drive later, unless `force` (fsync) is called and returns first. A torn last record is possible too, which is why logs carry a checksum per record, but the main point is that the OK went out before the payment was safe on the drive.

quiz.q: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` shows `Buffers: shared read=8000` for a query that finished in 30 ms, and the drives show no reads at all. How?
options: EXPLAIN counts the reads it planned, not the reads it did
The pages were in the buffer pool after all; `read` is a rounding error
`read` means the pages weren't in `shared_buffers`, so PostgreSQL asked the kernel, which had them in the operating system's page cache
The query ran on a copy of the database
quiz.why: PostgreSQL's buffer pool sits on top of the kernel's page cache, and it reads files through it. A miss in `shared_buffers` is counted as `read` even when the kernel hands over the page from memory in microseconds. That double caching is why `shared_buffers` starts near 25% of RAM rather than most of it.

quiz.q: A fraud check saves 50,000 small records a second, each under a random id (a UUID), and reads them back by id, rarely by range. Why might an LSM tree suit it better than a B+tree, and what does it pay?
options: The LSM tree writes sorted files in one long sequence instead of rewriting a random page per insert; it pays with compaction rewrites and reads that may check several files
The B+tree adds random ids at the end of its last leaf, so it wins on writes too
The LSM tree wins on writes and on reads, at no cost
The B+tree is better, because Bloom filters make its range scans fast
quiz.why: Random ids land on random leaf pages, so a B+tree rewrites (and logs) a whole 8 KB page for a small insert. An LSM tree collects writes in a sorted table in memory, the memtable, writes them out as one sorted file, and merges files in the background. It pays with the rewriting of compaction, and with lookups that may check several files, which Bloom filters make cheaper. Only ids that keep growing fill a B+tree's last leaf, and Bloom filters belong to LSM trees and don't help range scans.

quiz.q: The payments program commits a transfer between two balances and gets OK. A second later, the server loses power. The changed table pages were still dirty in the buffer pool. What does PostgreSQL find at restart?
options: The transfer is lost, because its pages never reached the data files
The data files are corrupt, and a backup must be restored
Half of the transfer, because pages are written one at a time
The transfer, because its log records were forced to disk at commit; recovery replays them onto the old pages from the last checkpoint
quiz.why: The commit rule says COMMIT returns only once the write-ahead log is on disk past the commit record; the pages can be written any time later. Recovery starts at the last checkpoint and reapplies every record whose log position (LSN) is newer than the page's, so the transfer comes back whole. Corruption is what `fsync = off` risks, not a normal power cut, and a torn page is restored from the full copy of it in the log.

quiz.q: A support screen finds the 10 past complaints most like a new one, for the same shop: `SELECT ... FROM complaints WHERE merchant_id = ? ORDER BY embedding <-> ? LIMIT 10`. It uses a pgvector HNSW index with default settings (pgvector adds search by meaning to PostgreSQL). For small shops it often shows 0 to 3 complaints, though they have dozens. What's going on?
options: The HNSW index is corrupt and needs a REINDEX
The index walk collects about 40 candidates and the WHERE clause runs afterwards, so a narrow filter leaves few rows; iterative scans, or a different index for the filter, fix it
LIMIT 10 is applied before the distance is worked out
HNSW can't index vectors from more than one shop
quiz.why: pgvector applies filters after the approximate walk. With `hnsw.ef_search` at 40, the walk returns 40 candidates by distance, and only the ones for that shop survive. `SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order` keeps walking until enough rows pass, and a partial index, or an exact search over the shop's few rows, also works. Nothing is broken, which is why the problem goes unnoticed.

quiz.q: A screen shows the 10 newest payments with their shops' names, and `merchants.id` (the shops table) has a primary-key index. A nightly report joins all 2 million payments with 10,000 shops. Which join suits each?
options: Hash join for both
Nested loop for both
Nested loop with the index for the screen (10 index lookups), hash join for the report (each table read once)
Merge join for both, because the primary key is sorted
quiz.why: With 10 outer rows, one index lookup per row touches a handful of pages; building a hash table of 10,000 shops first would cost more. For 2 million rows, a nested loop would do 2 million lookups or 20 billion comparisons, while a hash join builds a table of the shops once and looks up each payment in it.

quiz.q: Which statement about PostgreSQL's planner is true?
options: It picks the cheapest plan for its row-count guesses, which come from sampled statistics per column and assume that conditions on different columns are unrelated
It always finds the fastest plan, given an index
It runs the candidate plans on a sample and keeps the fastest
It learns how columns go together from indexes on several columns
quiz.why: The planner prices plans with a cost model fed by its row-count guesses, then searches the orders of joins by dynamic programming. The search is exact for what it's given, so when the plan is bad it's usually because a guess is far off, often from columns that go together. Only `CREATE STATISTICS` gives it statistics across columns; indexes don't.

quiz.q: Payments from 400 shops are written to Parquet files (a column-store file format) in the order they arrive. A monthly report filters on `merchant_id = 17` and one day, and the reader still reads every row group. What lets it skip most of them?
options: Bigger row groups, so there are fewer to read
zstd compression on top of the encodings
A B+tree index stored next to the file
Sorting each file by shop and day before writing it, so each row group's smallest and largest values cover a narrow range
quiz.why: A reader skips a row group when its column statistics, the smallest and largest value, rule out the condition. In arrival order, every row group holds most shops and days, so nothing can be ruled out. Sorted data gives each row group a narrow range that most queries miss. Compression and bigger groups make reads cheaper, but they don't skip anything.

quiz.q: A materialized view of each shop's daily totals over 200 million payments takes 6 minutes to refresh. The shops want it up to date within a minute of every payment. What fits?
options: Keep it up to date one change at a time: apply each payment as a delta (count + 1, sum + amount), with pg_ivm or a streaming view, so the work follows the change rather than all the payments
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW every 30 seconds
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY every 30 seconds, since it only applies the differences
Drop the view and work out the totals every time a page loads
quiz.why: A refresh, plain or concurrent, reruns the whole query, so it can't finish in 30 seconds when it needs 6 minutes; CONCURRENTLY applies the differences only after working everything out again. Count and sum have simple delta rules, so keeping them right costs one view row per payment. Working out the totals on every page load moves the 6 minutes onto the readers.

quiz.q: Thirty copies of the payments program each run a connection pool of 10 against a PostgreSQL server with `max_connections = 100` and 8 cores. New copies fail to connect. Which change addresses the cause?
options: Raise `max_connections` to 400 so every copy fits
Put PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode in front, so 300 client connections share a few dozen server processes, after checking the program keeps nothing in its sessions
Make the program's role a superuser so it can use the reserved slots
Lower `work_mem` so each connection uses less memory
quiz.why: Every PostgreSQL connection is a process forked by the postmaster. 300 processes on 8 cores fight for the processor even when the cap allows them, so raising it trades an error for a slower server. A pooler lets many client connections share a few busy server connections, one transaction at a time, and breaks only what a session keeps, such as `SET` without LOCAL, LISTEN and advisory locks. A superuser program is a security mistake, and work_mem doesn't change the count.
